Please review the following manuscript. I've poured months of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

import importlib.util, sys
print(sys.version)
for name in ('pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','pypdfium2','PIL'):
    spec = importlib.util.find_spec(name)
    print(name, spec.origin if spec else None)
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs
python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
with Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').open('w') as f:
    for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
        text = p.extract_text()
        f.write(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+text)
        print(i,len(text))
print(r.metadata)
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful setting: retrieving the same person from a reference image and a description of changed appearance, without training on composed-query triplets. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three source datasets.

The two-stage framework is straightforward and practical. Domain-specific CLIP fine-tuning followed by a lightweight textual inversion network enables composition through the text encoder. The diagrams, optimization equations, training settings, and supplementary timing results explain the approach reasonably well.

The reported improvements over simple composition are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.913% Rank-1 and 55.630% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for image–text feature averaging using the fine-tuned encoders. Improvements appear with both evaluated backbones.

The supplementary experiments provide useful evidence beyond the headline comparison, including loss functions, training-data quantity, network architecture, and ensemble configurations. Table B supports the benefit of identity-aware matching over instance-level contrastive training.
weaknesses: The comparison with the closest prior methods is materially confounded. Table 1 explicitly reuses Pic2Word and SEARLE mappings trained with original CLIP parameters alongside fine-tuned encoders, whereas Word4Per's mapping is trained for those encoders and person data. This can disadvantage the baselines through representation mismatch and unequal adaptation. Table B partially addresses this through an ITC ablation, but matched retraining of the competing methods is needed to substantiate the claimed advantage, particularly with ViT-L/14.

The held-out evaluation protocol is insufficiently established. ITCPR is described as exclusively a test set, yet Section 5.3 and Table 2 explicitly use retrieval performance to choose network architecture, prompt template, and token length. No separate composition validation set or independent selection procedure is specified. This risks optimistic results and weakens the claim of evaluation without using CPR annotations.

Methodological originality is limited relative to the cited literature. Mapping images into pseudo-word tokens for zero-shot composition is already central to Pic2Word and SEARLE; the encoder adaptation and matching objectives also largely reuse existing person-retrieval techniques. The task and benchmark are the more distinctive contributions, but the paper does not sufficiently isolate what its adaptations add beyond a carefully adapted prior pipeline.

Benchmark reliability needs stronger documentation. Appendix B.1 finds additional positives through a visual encoder's top-k retrieval, but does not specify the encoder, k, annotation agreement, or an audit of positives missed by that procedure. Consequently, ground-truth completeness remains uncertain. Per-source results and evaluation against similar-looking people would also help establish whether gains reflect reliable identity preservation.

Some implementation details obscure reproducibility. Table 1 labels the combined variant as a sum of losses, whereas Appendix C.4 describes fusion of separately trained networks. Equation 1 also includes vocabulary-size normalization that would strongly downweight the reasoning loss relative to the other objectives and needs confirmation. Run-to-run variability is not reported, making small architecture and fusion gains difficult to assess.

The public-security motivation and person-image benchmark warrant documentation of source-data reuse permissions and privacy protections, plus discussion of surveillance misuse and demographic performance limitations. These issues are not addressed; citing publicly available datasets does not by itself resolve them.
